newsitem.title: USA: U.S. EPA chief opposes Republican Superfund bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. EPA chief opposes Republican Superfund bill.

text.p: The Clinton administration and Senate Republicans Wednesday moved no closer than they were last year to reaching an agreement to improve the Superfund toxic waste cleanup program.

In her first testimony this year on the multibillion dollar program, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Carol Browner raised serious concerns about the latest Republican bill and said they should craft one from scratch.
"Why don't we pull out a blank sheet of paper and draft a Superfund reform bill that recognizes the progress we've made," she said.

She told the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee that the latest bill, introduced as one of the Senate Republicans' top 10 priorities for this year, did not reflect EPA's success in speeding up cleanups since 1992.

Congress has attempted but failed to reform the progam over the last several years, largely because the Republicans and Democrats disagree on who should be relieved from paying cleanup costs at sites where waste was dumped legally.
Cleanup liability at "co-disposal sites", where many people dumped waste, is one of the biggest sources of legal tangles that slows down Superfund cleanups.

To limit the litigation, the latest Senate Republican bill seeks to make the government pay all the cleanup costs at codisposal sites and cap the amount municipalities would have to pay to remove hazardous waste at garbage landfills.
But Browner said the bill's "numerous liability exemptions and limits basically reject the notion that polluters should pay their fair share to provide the funds for cleanup costs."

Committee chairman John Chafee tried to break the logjam telling Browner to stop accusing Republicans of "letting polluters off the hook" when the EPA itself had relieved small businesses and other groups from Superfund liability.
"It's all part of the same process. Just as you've removed some (polluters), we have," he said.
"I would appreciate it if you would take the expression 'letting polluters off the hook' and bottle it and throw it away somewhere," Chafee told Browner.
Browner said her problem with the Republican plan was that they would relieve any company based on where they dumped their waste, not based on how much of the problem they caused.
Browner raised concern about provisions that would let groundwater remain contaminated at a Superfund site if it was too costly to treat. Chafee said that issue could be resolved.
He said the Republicans would also be willing to address Browner's concerns that the worst problems, so-called hot spots, should not be exempt from cleanup treatments.
Browner also objected to the bill's attempt to take EPA out of the cleanup picture where states are able to take the lead on handling Superfund sites.
She said the bill should be more flexible in giving the federal government a role to ensure that public health and the environment were protected.
